# HyperQB fixtures

`divider_excerpt.txt` is a **trimmed excerpt** of real HyperQB 2.0 output,
captured from the web playground (https://hyperqb.egr.msu.edu/) running the
bundled Verilog divider benchmark with `-k 8 -s pes -c`.

Trimmed how: the original had 9 state blocks with ~50 signals each. Three
blocks were kept and renumbered 0..2 so the excerpt is still a contiguous
`State 0..k`, and the signal list was cut down. Every *format* feature of the
original is preserved verbatim:

  - all four value encodings: `true` / `false` / `#b<bits>` / `#x<hex>`
  - signal names containing underscores and digits (`s_input_b_ack`, `a_e`)
  - a **partial model**: `input_b` appears at state 0 and not at state 1
  - the surrounding `[IR]` / timing / `result:` / `Solve Time:` lines

The parser is tested against this rather than against invented text, because
the name-splitting rule (only a trailing `_<digits>_<UPPER>` is structure) is
exactly the kind of thing that is easy to get wrong from a written spec.

---

`simple_buffer_od.txt` is a **complete, unedited** HyperQB 2.0 run, produced
locally by:

    HyperRUSTY -n simple_buffer.smv simple_buffer.smv -f simple_buffer.hq \
               -k 4 -s pes -c

where `simple_buffer.hq` was generated by `frontends/_formula.HyperQbRenderer`
from the same `-f` s-expression the internal engine uses. The property is
observational determinism, `G(out[A] = out[B])`, and it fails.

Note `State 4` omits `secret` entirely -- the solver never constrained it, so
the model is genuinely partial even on a five-state example.
